1.title: Getting Started
1.study: Start with CS50P Week 0/your Python setup. Install Python, VS Code and a virtual environment; learn how to run a .py file and a notebook.
1.credential: Harvard CS50P Certificate — complete the full course + final project (certificate is course-level, not per lesson).
1.read: CS50P — Introduction to Programming with Python
1.project: Create a clean Python repo with a README, requirements file and one runnable script.
1.revision: Recall: terminal, interpreter, script vs notebook, virtual environment.
1.output: Working Python environment + first Git repo.
1.why: This removes setup friction before every later section.

2.title: Python Programming Language
2.study: Study variables, data types, strings, operators, input/output and basic expressions. Code every example yourself.
2.credential: Kaggle Python Course Certificate — free completion certificate.
2.project: Build a console mini-program that accepts data, validates it and prints a useful report.
2.output: Python syntax cheat sheet + 1 mini program.
2.why: Every later data/ML library assumes this fluency.

3.title: Python Control Flow
3.study: Master if/elif/else, nested conditions, for/while loops, break, continue and range.
3.credential: Kaggle Python certificate checkpoint; the certificate is for the course, so use your Section 3 practice as evidence.
3.project: Solve 15 loop/condition problems without looking at solutions.
3.why: Control flow is the foundation for writing preprocessing and training logic.

4.title: Inbuilt Data Structures in Python
4.study: Learn list, tuple, set, dictionary, indexing, slicing, mutability and common methods. Practice nested structures.
4.credential: Kaggle Python certificate checkpoint; add a data-structures notebook as proof.
4.project: Build a contact/inventory manager using dictionaries + lists with search/update/delete.
4.why: Pandas, preprocessing pipelines and JSON work depend heavily on these structures.

5.title: Functions in Python
5.study: Learn function definition, parameters, arguments, return values, default parameters and local/global scope.
5.credential: Harvard CS50P Certificate — use the section practice now; claim the free course certificate after all required work.
5.read: CS50P — functions, arguments and return values
5.project: Refactor a previous mini-program into reusable functions with tests.
5.why: ML code becomes much cleaner when you can decompose work into functions.

6.title: Function Practice Questions
6.study: Do practice first. Write functions from a blank file: string processing, list processing, searching, counting and validation.
6.credential: No reputable standalone free certificate for isolated practice; use GitHub problem-solving evidence + Kaggle Python course certificate.
6.project: Create a single public repo with 20 clean Python solutions and explanations.
6.why: This is where syntax turns into actual programming ability.

7.title: Inbuilt Data Structure — Practice Questions
7.study: Practice list/dict/set transformations, frequency maps, sorting, deduplication and nested data extraction.
7.credential: No standalone free certificate; use the problem set as proof and finish Kaggle Python if not already done.
7.project: Solve 15 data-structure exercises and explain time complexity for at least five.
7.why: Efficient data manipulation is essential for EDA and feature engineering.

8.title: Importing, Creating Modules and Packages
8.study: Understand import, from-import, __name__ == '__main__', package layout, pip and virtual environments.
8.credential: Harvard CS50P certificate checkpoint; no isolated certificate for modules.
8.project: Turn one earlier project into a package with separate modules for input, logic and output.
8.why: Production ML repositories must be modular rather than one giant notebook.

9.title: File Handling in Python
9.study: Read/write text, CSV and JSON; understand with/open, paths and basic data serialization.
9.credential: No standalone reputable free certificate; use project evidence + CS50P completion later.
9.read: Python official tutorial — input and output
9.project: Build a CSV/JSON ingestion script that validates rows and produces a clean output file.
9.why: Nearly every real ML pipeline starts with reading and validating data.

10.title: Exception Handling in Python
10.study: Learn try/except/else/finally, raising exceptions and creating meaningful error messages.
10.credential: No standalone reputable free certificate; use robust project + CS50P completion later.
10.read: Python official tutorial — errors and exceptions
10.project: Add validation and custom exceptions to your data-ingestion project.
10.why: Production services must fail clearly instead of silently breaking.

11.title: OOPS Concepts with Classes and Objects
11.study: Master classes, objects, __init__, instance/class variables, inheritance, composition and polymorphism.
11.credential: Harvard CS50P certificate; no isolated OOP certificate is required.
11.project: Model a small ML domain: Dataset, Model, Trainer and Evaluator classes.
11.why: Flask, ML tooling and larger Python codebases become much easier after OOP.

12.title: Advanced Python
12.study: Learn comprehensions, lambda, iterators, generators, decorators, context managers and practical functional patterns.
12.credential: No standalone certificate; use CS50P certificate + advanced-Python project evidence.
12.project: Write a mini data pipeline using a generator, decorator and context manager.
12.why: These ideas appear later in data pipelines, logging and production utilities.

13.title: Data Analysis with Python
13.study: Learn NumPy arrays, Pandas DataFrames, filtering, groupby, merges, missing values and visualization.
13.credential: Kaggle Python + Pandas + Data Visualization course certificates; all Kaggle Learn courses provide completion certificates.
13.read: Python Data Analysis with Pandas — practical reference
13.project: Analyze one real CSV end-to-end and produce an EDA notebook with at least 8 useful plots/tables.
13.why: This is the bridge from Python programming to Data Science.

14.title: Working with SQLite3
14.study: Learn SQLite connection, CREATE/INSERT/SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE, parameterized queries and commit/close.
14.credential: No strong standalone free SQLite certification; use SQLite project proof.
14.project: Convert your previous CRUD project to a clean SQLite-backed application.
14.why: Flask and real applications need persistent data storage.

15.title: Logging in Python
15.study: Learn logger levels, handlers, formatters, log files and why print() is not production logging.
15.credential: No standalone free credential; use a GitHub project with structured logging as proof.
15.project: Replace print statements in a project with logging to console + file, including error logs.
15.why: Logging becomes critical for deployment, debugging and MLOps.

16.title: Python Multi Threading and Multi Processing
16.study: Understand threads vs processes, CPU-bound vs I/O-bound tasks, locks, pools and when concurrency helps.
16.credential: No standalone free credential; use an implementation benchmark as proof.
16.project: Benchmark sequential vs threaded vs multiprocessing execution on a suitable workload.
16.why: Useful later for APIs, ETL and data-processing services.

17.title: Memory Management with Python
17.study: Understand object references, mutability, garbage collection, reference counting and practical memory profiling.
17.credential: No standalone free credential; use a memory-profiling mini-project as proof.
17.project: Profile a script, identify a memory-heavy pattern and optimize it.
17.why: This gives you better intuition before production ML and containers.

18.title: Getting Started with Flask Framework
18.study: Primary: Udemy Section 18. Supplement with Corey Schafer Flask. Build routes, templates/forms, CRUD and app structure.
18.credential: No strong official free standalone Flask certification; use a deployed Flask project + GitHub as proof. Do not buy a random 'Flask certificate'.
18.project: Build a Flask CRUD API + SQLite backend and deploy it locally with a clean README.
18.revision: Review Python OOP, modules, SQLite, logging and exceptions.
18.why: Flask is your bridge from ML notebook code to an application/API.

19.title: Getting Started with Streamlit Web Framework
19.credential: No strong standalone free Streamlit certification; use a deployed dashboard as proof.
19.project: Turn your Flask/EDA/ML output into an interactive Streamlit dashboard.
19.why: Fastest route from Python code to a usable ML demo.

20.title: Getting Started with Statistics
20.credential: IBM SkillsBuild Data Analytics pathway — Introduction to Inferential and Descriptive Statistics digital credential.
20.project: Write a statistical report on one dataset.
20.why: Stats decides whether model results mean anything.

21.title: Introduction to Probability
21.credential: IBM SkillsBuild statistics credential; probability is supporting knowledge rather than a separate credential.
21.project: Build a Monte Carlo simulator for coins, dice and conditional events.
21.why: Probability supports Bayesian reasoning and ML uncertainty.

22.title: Probability Distribution Functions for Data
22.project: Compare normal, binomial, Poisson and exponential distributions on simulated/real data.
22.why: Distributional assumptions matter throughout statistics and ML.

23.title: Inferential Statistics
23.credential: IBM SkillsBuild Inferential & Descriptive Statistics digital credential.
23.read: ASA Statement on Statistical Significance and P-Values
23.project: Run one A/B test with confidence interval, p-value and a plain-English conclusion.
23.why: This keeps you from making statistically weak ML claims.

24.title: Feature Engineering
24.credential: Kaggle Feature Engineering certificate — no-cost completion certificate.
24.read: An Introduction to Variable and Feature Selection — Guyon & Elisseeff
24.project: Create and benchmark at least 10 features on one tabular dataset.
24.why: Good features often matter more than switching algorithms.

25.title: Exploratory Data Analysis and Feature Engineering
25.credential: Kaggle Data Cleaning + Data Visualization certificates.
25.project: Publish a full EDA report: data quality, distributions, outliers, relationships and actionable findings.
25.why: EDA is where you discover what the dataset is really saying.

26.title: Introduction to Machine Learning
26.credential: Kaggle Intro to Machine Learning certificate.
26.read: A Few Useful Things to Know About Machine Learning — Pedro Domingos
26.project: Train a baseline model and document the end-to-end ML workflow.
26.why: You need the workflow before individual algorithms.

27.title: Complete Linear Regression — Intuition & Practicals
27.credential: Kaggle Intro to Machine Learning certificate as the formal free ML credential; project proves regression skill.
27.read: An Introduction to Statistical Learning, Chapter 3
27.project: Build a house-price regression system and analyze residuals/metrics.
27.why: Regression teaches the core optimization/statistics mindset.

28.title: Ridge, Lasso and ElasticNet
28.credential: Kaggle Intermediate ML / Feature Engineering certificate + project evidence.
28.read: The Elements of Statistical Learning — regularization sections
28.project: Compare Linear/Ridge/Lasso/ElasticNet and explain coefficient changes.
28.why: Regularization controls overfitting and feature redundancy.

29.title: Steps by Step Project Implementation with Life Cycle of ML Project
29.credential: No standalone free certificate; use a production-style ML repo as proof.
29.read: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems — Sculley et al.
29.project: Refactor one ML project into data/preprocessing/training/evaluation/inference modules.
29.why: This is the transition from notebook ML to engineering.

30.title: Logistic Regression
30.credential: Kaggle Intro/Intermediate ML certificate + project proof.
30.read: The Regression Analysis of Binary Sequences — Cox (1958)
30.project: Build a churn/medical-risk classifier and report precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC.

31.title: Support Vector Machines
31.credential: Project proof; no strong standalone free SVM credential needed.
31.project: Compare linear vs RBF SVM with proper feature scaling.
31.why: Teaches margins, kernels and the geometry of classification.

32.title: Naive Bayes Theorem
32.read: On the Optimality of the Simple Bayesian Classifier under Zero-One Loss — Domingos & Pazzani
32.project: Build a spam classifier and inspect class probabilities.
32.why: Fast, interpretable baseline for text problems.

33.title: K Nearest Neighbour ML Algorithm
33.read: Nearest Neighbor Pattern Classification — Cover & Hart
33.project: Tune K and visualize validation performance.
33.why: Shows why distance and feature scaling matter.

34.title: Decision Tree Classifier and Regressor
34.project: Build a decision tree and visualize/interpret splits.
34.why: Interpretability and nonlinear splits become intuitive here.

35.title: Random Forest Machine Learning
35.credential: Kaggle Intro/Intermediate ML certificate + project evidence.
35.project: Compare one tree vs Random Forest and inspect feature importance.
35.why: A strong tabular baseline and foundation for boosting.

36.title: AdaBoost Machine Learning Algorithm
36.read: A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting — Freund & Schapire
36.project: Compare a weak tree to AdaBoost; inspect how mistakes get reweighted.

37.title: Gradient Boosting
37.read: Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine — Friedman
37.project: Change learning rate/depth and observe validation behavior.
37.why: This is the conceptual bridge to XGBoost.

38.title: XGBoost Machine Learning Algorithms
38.study: Udemy + XGBoost docs + Kaggle Intermediate ML.
38.credential: Kaggle Intermediate Machine Learning certificate — no-cost.
38.read: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System — Chen & Guestrin
38.project: Run a small tabular competition workflow with CV, feature engineering and leakage checks.

39.title: Unsupervised Machine Learning
39.read: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning — Bishop, clustering chapters
39.project: Take an unlabeled dataset and frame a clustering question.
39.why: Teaches you to reason without a target variable.

40.title: PCA
40.credential: Kaggle Feature Engineering certificate includes PCA; use it as formal credential.
40.read: A tutorial on Principal Component Analysis — Shlens
40.project: Reduce a high-dimensional dataset to 2D/3D and explain variance retained.
40.why: Dimensionality reduction is essential for visualization and some pipelines.

41.title: K Means Clustering Unsupervised ML
41.credential: Kaggle Feature Engineering certificate + project proof.
41.read: Least Squares Quantization in PCM — Lloyd
41.project: Build customer segmentation and justify your chosen K.
41.why: Classic clustering algorithm with strong practical value.

42.title: Hierarchical Clustering
42.project: Create dendrograms and compare linkage strategies.
42.why: Useful when you want a hierarchy instead of one flat partition.

43.title: DBSCAN Clustering
43.read: A Density-Based Algorithm for Discovering Clusters in Large Spatial Databases — Ester et al.
43.project: Cluster spatial/synthetic data and label noise points.
43.why: Handles arbitrary shapes and explicit noise much better than KMeans.

44.title: Silhouette Clustering
44.read: Silhouettes: A graphical aid to the interpretation and validation of cluster analysis — Rousseeuw
44.project: Compare multiple K values with silhouette score and explain the choice.
44.why: You need objective evidence for your clustering choice.

45.title: Anomaly Detection Machine Learning Algorithms
45.read: Anomaly Detection: A Survey — Chandola, Banerjee & Kumar
45.project: Build an anomaly detector and discuss false positives/negatives.
45.why: Useful for fraud, security and monitoring.

46.title: Docker for Beginners
46.study: Udemy + Docker docs + IBM cloud fundamentals.
46.credential: No official free Docker certification I would recommend. Use IBM SkillsBuild Cloud Computing Fundamentals credential (includes Docker/container practice) as the adjacent formal credential.
46.cert_type: Formal free adjacent credential + project proof
46.read: An Introduction to Docker for Reproducible Research — Boettiger
46.project: Dockerize an ML API: Dockerfile, image, container, port mapping and env vars.
46.why: Containers are the packaging layer for reproducible deployment.

47.title: GIT for Beginners
47.credential: GitHub Skills for hands-on proof; GitHub also has current credentials/certifications, but the certification exams are not a free substitute for learning.
47.project: Put one strong ML project through branch → commit → PR → merge → tag → release.
47.why: Version control is non-negotiable for engineering.

48.title: End to End Machine Learning Project with AWS/Azure Deployment
48.credential: AWS Training badges / AWS Cloud Quest are free to earn for eligible paths; use a relevant cloud/ML badge after completing the project.
48.cert_type: Formal free AWS badge + project proof
48.read: ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness — Breck et al.
48.project: Deploy a real ML service from dataset to API to Docker to cloud.
48.why: This is the first point where your model is actually serving users.

49.title: End to End MLOps Projects with ETL Pipelines
49.study: Udemy + AWS SimuLearn MLOps/ML + MLOps literature.
49.credential: AWS SimuLearn badges are currently available for Machine Learning and other domains and issue verifiable Credly badges.
49.cert_type: Formal free AWS badge + project proof
49.read: Machine Learning Operations (MLOps): Overview, Definition, and Architecture — Kreuzberger et al.
49.project: Build ETL → validation → training → tracking → deployment → monitoring, with a security-aware data flow.
49.revision: Review Docker, Git and cloud deployment.
49.why: This is the strongest engineering section of the course.

50.title: ML Flow + Dash + BentoML — Complete ML Project Lifecycle
50.credential: Project proof; use the Section 49 AWS badge as your cloud credential rather than chasing a random MLflow certificate.
50.read: Accelerating the Machine Learning Lifecycle with MLflow — Zaharia et al.
50.project: Connect MLflow tracking → registry → BentoML serving → Dash monitoring.
50.output: Tracked, served and monitored ML project.
50.why: This is the architecture pattern recruiters expect from MLOps work.

51.title: NLP for Machine Learning
51.credential: Hugging Face learning certificates where offered; use course/chapter completion as supplementary proof, not a professional certification.
51.read: Speech and Language Processing — Jurafsky & Martin
51.project: Build a sentiment/spam/intent classifier with text preprocessing and evaluation.
51.why: This establishes classical NLP before neural NLP.

52.title: Deep Learning
52.study: Udemy + Kaggle Intro to Deep Learning.
52.credential: Kaggle Intro to Deep Learning certificate — no-cost.
52.project: Train a neural network and document training/validation curves.
52.why: You need the math/optimization intuition before RNNs and Transformers.

53.title: End to End Deep Learning Project using ANN
53.credential: Kaggle Intro to Deep Learning certificate + GitHub/deployed project proof.
53.read: Learning representations by back-propagating errors — Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams
53.project: Turn the ANN into a complete application with preprocessing, training and inference.

54.title: NLP with Deep Learning
54.credential: Hugging Face learning certificate(s) where offered + project proof.
54.read: Natural Language Processing (Almost) from Scratch — Collobert et al.
54.project: Build a neural text classifier with embeddings.
54.why: Shows the move from hand-crafted features to learned representations.

55.title: Simple RNN In-depth Intuition
55.credential: Project proof; no need for a separate certificate.
55.project: Build a small character-level RNN and inspect sequence behavior.
55.why: Teaches recurrence before gates and attention.

56.title: End to End Deep Learning Project with Simple RNN
56.read: On the Difficulty of Training Recurrent Neural Networks — Pascanu et al.
56.project: Train an RNN for text/sequence prediction and analyze failure modes.
56.why: You should experience vanishing gradients rather than only hearing about them.

57.title: LSTM and GRU RNN In-depth Intuition
57.credential: Project proof; Hugging Face learning evidence is optional.
57.project: Compare Simple RNN vs LSTM vs GRU.
57.why: This is the conceptual prerequisite to understanding old seq2seq systems.

58.title: LSTM and GRU End to End Deep Learning Project — Predicting Next Word
58.credential: Project proof + Hugging Face learning progress.
58.read: Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation — Cho et al.
58.project: Build a next-word predictor with your own small corpus.
58.why: Makes sequence modeling concrete before encoder-decoder/attention.

59.title: Bidirectional RNN Architecture and Intuition
59.read: Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks — Schuster & Paliwal
59.project: Compare uni-directional vs bidirectional text classification.
59.why: Shows how future context can help when the full sequence is known.

60.title: Encoder Decoder | Sequence to Sequence Architecture
60.credential: Hugging Face course progress/certificate where applicable + project proof.
60.read: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks — Sutskever, Vinyals & Le
60.why: This is the direct predecessor to attention + Transformers.

61.title: Attention Mechanism — Seq2Seq Networks
61.credential: Project proof + Hugging Face learning evidence.
61.read: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate — Bahdanau et al.
61.project: Visualize attention weights and explain what tokens the model focuses on.
61.why: This is the key idea that leads directly to Transformers.

62.title: Transformers
62.study: Udemy + original Transformer paper + Hugging Face.
62.credential: Hugging Face LLM Course end-of-chapter certificate(s) where offered; certificates are learning credentials, not professional certification.
62.read: Attention Is All You Need — Vaswani et al.
62.project: Implement or fine-tune a Transformer-based task and explain Q/K/V, multi-head attention, positional encoding, residuals and normalization.
62.why: This is the most important research checkpoint for modern NLP/GenAI.

63.title: Claude Code — Vibe Coding for Developers
63.study: Udemy + Anthropic official engineering/Claude Code material.
63.credential: No credible free 'Claude Code certificate' worth putting above project evidence. Use official learning material + GitHub project demonstrating the workflow.
63.read: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
63.project: Use an AI coding agent on a real repo: understand → plan → test → implement → review → document.
63.why: The value is demonstrating controlled engineering, not prompt tricks.

64.title: Role Play
64.study: Use the entire roadmap as interview preparation.
64.credential: No certificate required; this is your final internal assessment and portfolio defense.
64.read: Re-read: Hidden Technical Debt + Attention Is All You Need + SWE-bench + your own project reports.
64.resource: Your own GitHub portfolio + mock interview
64.project: 30-minute ML/AI Engineer mock interview + 30-minute system-design walkthrough of your best deployed project.
64.revision: Cumulative revision of the entire roadmap.

Arrays & Hashing: Watch 1 NeetCode explanation before attempting a new pattern
Solve Mediums with a 20–30 min attempt limit
After the section, take the 10-question checkpoint
Re-solve missed problems after 1 day and 7 days
Two Pointers: Understand when the array is sorted / when pointers move toward each other
Learn the pointer invariant before coding
Do Valid Palindrome first as the template
Treat Trapping Rain Water as a later challenge
Checkpoint: 10 mixed Two Pointer + earlier Array questions
Sliding Window: Identify what is inside the window
Choose the state you must maintain: count/set/max/min
Treat Minimum Window and Maximum as Hard patterns
Stack: Understand LIFO and when a stack removes nested/previous state
Use Valid Parentheses as the base template
Binary Search: Use Time Based KV for binary-search-on-time
Leave Median of Two Sorted Arrays for last
Linked List: Draw nodes and arrows before coding
Master traversal, reversal and fast/slow pointers
Tries: Understand prefix nodes and child maps
Then combine Trie + Backtracking for Word Search II
Heap / Priority Queue: Do Kth Largest Stream + Last Stone
Then K Closest and Task Scheduler
Graphs: Learn adjacency list and visited set
Advanced Graphs: Learn shortest paths: BFS vs Dijkstra
Compare binary search on answer vs Dijkstra
Finish Alien Dictionary and K Stops
1-D Dynamic Programming: Define the state in one sentence
2-D Dynamic Programming: Then state-machine DP and interval DP
Leave hardest problems to the end
Greedy: First ask whether a local choice can be proven safe
Start with Maximum Subarray and Jump Game
Write a short proof beside your code
Intervals: Sort by start or end first
Math & Geometry: Look for invariants and coordinate transforms
